title: Former Indian Army Chief General VN Sharma Dies at 96
excerpt: General Vishwa Nath Sharma, the first president's commissioned officer to lead the Indian Army, served as Chief of Army Staff from 1988 to 1990 and stood firm during the 1987 Wangdung crisis with China.
body:
• General Vishwa Nath Sharma, India's 14th Chief of Army Staff, died in New Delhi on July 31, 2026, at the age of 96
  • He was the first president's commissioned officer to lead the Indian Army, having been commissioned in June 1950
  • As Eastern Command chief, he defied orders to withdraw from forward positions during the 1987 Wangdung standoff with China
  • His elder brother, Major Somnath Sharma, was the first recipient of India's highest military honor, the Param Vir Chakra

A Military Legacy Spanning Four Decades

General Vishwa Nath Sharma, who served as India's 14th Chief of Army Staff from 1988 to 1990, died in New Delhi on Thursday at the age of 96. His death marks the passing of one of India's most consequential military leaders, a cavalryman whose career spanned the formative decades of the Indian Army's post-independence evolution.

https://x.com/rajnathsingh/status/2083092005610254732

Born on June 4, 1930, in London to Major General Amar Nath Sharma, a military doctor, Sharma came from a family with an extraordinary record of military service. His elder brother, Major Somnath Sharma, was the first and first posthumous recipient of the Param Vir Chakra, India's highest wartime gallantry award. Another brother, Lieutenant General Surindra Nath Sharma, served as Engineer-in-Chief of the Indian Army.

Sharma was commissioned into the 16th Light Cavalry on June 4, 1950, making him part of the first cohort of officers commissioned by the president of the Indian republic rather than by the British Crown. He fought in the 1965 Indo-Pakistani War in the Lahore sector, commanded the 66th Armoured Regiment, and later led a mountain brigade in an insurgency-affected area before rising through the ranks to lead Eastern Command and eventually the entire Indian Army.

The Wangdung Crisis That Defined His Career

General Sharma's most defining moment came during the 1987 Wangdung incident, a tense military standoff with China that is considered the third Sino-Indian military conflict since independence. When the People's Liberation Army occupied the village of Wangdung in the Sumdorong Chu area of Arunachal Pradesh's Tawang district in 1986, Sharma, then the General Officer Commanding-in-Chief of Eastern Command, took a stance that would become a turning point in India-China border relations.

"Army HQ wanted me to withdraw from Wangdung in 1987 but I refused."

— General VN Sharma, in an interview with The Caravan magazine

According to Sharma's own account, he refused orders from Army Headquarters and the then Chief of Army Staff, General Krishnaswamy Sundarji, to vacate forward positions that the Indian Army had occupied opposite the PLA. The positions were near the strategically sensitive Thagla Ridge, the same location that had precipitated the disastrous 1962 Sino-Indian conflict. Sharma's decision to hold ground is widely credited with strengthening India's strategic posture along the Line of Actual Control.

Post-Military Service and Legacy

After retiring from the army in 1990, Sharma served on the boards of several institutions, including ABN AMRO's Local Advisory Board of India and Hawkins Cookers Limited. He remained an active member of the Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses and the United Services Institute of India until his death. From 2006 to 2009, he served on India's National Security Advisory Board.

The Sharma family also maintained a Free Tuberculosis and Medical Centre in their ancestral village of Dadh in Himachal Pradesh's Kangra district, which operated from 1992 until the general's death. The family hailed from the same village, and both Vishwa Nath and his brothers were educated at the Prince of Wales' Royal Indian Military College in Dehradun and Sherwood College in Nainital.

Decorated with the Param Vishisht Seva Medal and Ati Vishisht Seva Medal, General Sharma's four-decade military career encompassed service in the Nagaland and Mizoram insurgencies, both Indo-Pakistani Wars of 1965 and 1971, and the Indian Peace Keeping Force operations of 1987. His passing severs a living link to the earliest years of the Indian republic's military establishment.
